startup.name: Blueshoe
startup.one_liner: The AI-Native Consumer + Plaintiff Law Firm
startup.description: Blueshoe is a full-stack AI-native law firm for consumers and plaintiffs. People get legal guidance from a web app or through AI assistants, and when representation is needed Blueshoe attorneys take cases through to resolution with AI tools and operational support. Revenue would come from contingency fees on plaintiff cases and fees for consumer matters. Two founders, San Francisco, Spring 2025 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: The company is already in the Spring 2025 batch, so this is a note only. A random applicant starts near 1 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md). A law firm model run by two founders is unusual, and ownership rules for law firms limit outside investors, which would pull a cold application down, while the plaintiff AI theme and a clear paying customer type pull it up.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because a firm that owns case outcomes is a services business with contingency risk and licensing limits, not software. Reviewers would ask whether two founders include a licensed trial lawyer, how cases are sourced, and why this is not simply a lawyer using ChatGPT.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Window is 19.3 months, from 2025-04-07 to 2026-11-17. The anchor is an ever number; the time to milestones table (era 2022+) has a seed median of 6 months and a 75th percentile of 14 months, so most eventual seed raisers have raised by 19 months, and I take about 0.85 of the anchor. Legal AI funding is hot, but a law firm has ownership limits and a small team, so I do not lift above the anchor. The odds do not rank this company against others.

ladder.why_it_fails: The seed stalls if investors treat a two person firm as a services business: contingency fee revenue is lumpy and arrives years after a case is signed, and state rules on who may own a law firm limit equity investors. Plaintiff AI tooling vendors such as Eve and Supio raised large rounds as software, so money flows to tools rather than to firms. Spire Law, the closest firm analog, never raised past the YC deal.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A inside 19 months would need a signed case inventory with proven settlement economics, which needs a full case cycle of 18 to 36 months. Investors would also want a software layer that scales without more lawyers. Darrow reached a Series A as a data and case sourcing tool sold to firms, not as a firm itself, which shows which shape of this business gets funded.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C and later requires a national platform in a regulated profession, and ownership rules for law firms vary by state and constrain structure. Reaching it would need a licensed entity arrangement that growth investors accept, and a repeatable intake engine in several states. Few analogs in the data come close to that.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most paths end in a small practice or a stall. A two person firm can be profitable and still stay too small for venture returns, as Spire Law did. A shutdown follows if early cases settle slowly while the team pays for intake and malpractice cover, or if general AI assistants give consumers free legal answers before they need a firm.

killers.risk: The firm model scares equity investors and runs into ownership rules
killers.evidence: Spire Law, the closest firm analog, stayed a small practice with no post YC round; money in plaintiff AI went to software vendors such as Eve and Supio.
killers.mitigation: Build the software and data layer as a separate licensable asset and use a compliant structure with a managing attorney.

killers.risk: Contingency cash arrives too slowly to fund the team
killers.evidence: Personal injury cases take 12 to 36 months to settle, and intake costs are paid up front.
killers.mitigation: Mix fast fee consumer matters with plaintiff cases and use litigation finance.

killers.risk: Free general AI assistants capture the consumer legal question
killers.evidence: Consumers already ask general assistants legal questions, and the product's front door is a chat interface.
killers.mitigation: Win on representation and trial, which assistants cannot do.

killers.risk: Well funded plaintiff AI vendors move into firm ownership or alliances
killers.evidence: Eve raised $47M in January 2025 and Supio raised a Series A, both aiming at plaintiff firms.
killers.mitigation: Pick a case type where the firm owns proprietary outcome data.

technical_complexity.rationale: The software part is a case intake and drafting app that two engineers can build in three months with current models. The hard part is not technical: it is law firm licensing, case sourcing, malpractice cover and winning cases, none of which a small team can speed up with code.

takeover_risk.rationale: Funded tool vendors can add consumer facing features quickly, and big firms can adopt tools themselves. A law firm model is harder to copy because of licensing, so the risk is moderate.

evidence.claim: Plaintiff side legal AI drew large rounds in 2024 and 2025 (Eve $47M, Supio Series A), showing firms pay for tools that raise case throughput.
Personal injury firms already pay for case workflow software, the status quo that AI replaces.

roadmap.goal: A visible case pipeline with settled results.
actions: Sign a steady flow of consumer and plaintiff matters through a compliant entity.
Publish cycle time and settlement metrics against typical firms.
roadmap.proof: Dozens of signed cases and the first settlements, with cost per case below the traditional average.

actions: Raise revenue per lawyer through automation of intake and drafting.
Open a second case type or state.
roadmap.proof: Revenue per attorney well above peers with stable margins.

pros.point: Plaintiff AI is a funded, fast moving category
pros.evidence: Eve, Supio and Finch all raised from top funds in 2024 and 2025.

pros.point: The firm owns the customer relationship and outcome data
pros.evidence: A firm gets case outcome data that tool vendors only see in part, which can power better intake and pricing.

narrative.headline: An interesting firm shaped bet in a hot plaintiff AI market, with a coin flip on a seed over 19 months and long odds beyond.
narrative.general_summary: Blueshoe is a law firm run with AI tools, serving consumers and plaintiffs. Plaintiff AI tooling has raised large rounds, which helps sentiment, but the money has gone to software vendors, and the closest firm analog, Spire Law, never raised past the YC deal. The seed estimate for the 19 month window sits near the B2B cohort anchor and does not rank this company against others. A Series A inside the window is unlikely because case cycles are long. The path that worked in the data was Darrow's, a software and data business sold to firms. A pivot toward licensable software is the main upside route.

assumptions: Blind forecast as of 2025-04-07, using only the description file and market searches.
Window from 2025-04-07 to 2026-11-17 is 19.3 months. Seed means a financing above about $1M from outside investors that closes inside the window; series_a given seed is for the same window.
Funding anchors use the 2022-2025 B2B cohort, which is right censored; the ever rate is discounted for the window using the time to milestones table.
Two founders; whether either is a licensed attorney is unknown and assumed.
